content.title: Netflix ready to embark on MLB journey with Opening Night matchup
content.text: The Netflix Epic building in Los Angeles, California, US, on Thursday, Oct. 3, 2024. Photographer: Kyle Grillot/Bloomberg via Getty Images Bloomberg via Getty Images Netflix’s partnership with MLB starts Wednesday night with Yankees-Giants Opening Night, part of a three-event package for the streaming service, according to Joe Reedy of the AP. MLB Network will produce the game with Matt Vasgersian on play-by-play, Baseball HOF inductee CC Sabathia and former MLBer Hunter Pence as the analysts and Lauren Shehadi as a reporter. Netflix’s Elle Duncan will host pregame and postgame coverage. She will be joined by former MLBers Barry Bonds, Albert Pujols and Anthony Rizzo. The rest of Netflix’s streaming lineup includes the Home Run Derby and Field of Dreams game with the Twins-Phillies on Aug. 13 (AP, 3/23). In L.A., Cerys Davies notes the three-year deal Netflix has for the various events that pay MLB $60M annually will help inform the streamer “about whether to pursue a larger package when the league’s larger media rights contract, which includes the World Series on Fox, comes up for renewal after the 2028 season.” Meanwhile, the Yankees-Giants opener marks the “first time an MLB opening day game will be seen globally, as Netflix reaches nearly a billion viewers in more than 190 countries and in 50 languages” (L.A. TIMES, 3/25).INSIDE NETFLIX’S VISION: Netflix VP/Live Sports Gabe Spitzer emphasized that Netflix “is ‘in the event business more than the live sports volume business,’” and drew upon his experience as a documentary filmmaker to “present a vision that appealed to MLB.” He said, “It really comes down to characters. You’re telling a story, whether you’re watching a live game or you’re doing a documentary.” Spitzer added, “You want to feel like if you’re a viewer you’re inside and you’re learning something new. That story could be the ebb and flow of a game, it could be the backstory of a player that you might have never heard of and now you’re rooting for him” (S.F. CHRONICLE, 3/23).THE REVOLUTION WILL NOT BE TELEVISED: In Akron, George Thomas notes Yankees-Giants is the “first season opener to come exclusively to a streaming platform,” the latest sign that sports television’s “future is now.” Netflix’s jump into MLB follows the company’s strategy “to stream sporting events of significance, including Christmas NFL games.” However, fans “should not miss the forest for the trees,” as streaming is “not the future in its entirety.” Games on broadcast television will not disappear completely, as the “more partners you have the more checks you can bank.” What it does do is “play into a larger shift ... seen in society in the past two decades.” There will be fans who “won’t shrug at coughing up cash to stream or watch top-tier sporting events” and others who “will be limited in what games they have access” (AKRON BEACON JOURNAL, 3/25).HOW MUCH ARE YOU WILLING TO PAY? THE ATHLETIC’s Andrew Marchand notes the growth of digital outlets airing small packages of games means Yankees fans will “need access to eight networks for the full 162-game slate, plus potentially two more if the Yankees make the playoffs.” The associated costs are “nearly $800 for the season” using the minimum subscription costs for accessing games. For all that money spent on live sports, viewers “get a heap of frustration: Not knowing where to find their games daily; not enjoying their non-local broadcasters; and having to manage all those recurring bills.” Yankees President and YES Network Chair Randy Levine said that the “networks, leagues and new platforms understand the problem.” However, Marchand notes the issue is that “everyone wants to dominate the post-cable, direct-to-consumer landscape” (THE ATHLETIC, 3/25).Sponsored contentAdditional SectionsAwards & HonorsBettingCollegesDataEvents and Attractions Exec TransactionsFacilitiesFinanceFranchisesInternationalLabor and AgentsLeagues and Governing BodiesLegal and GovernanceMarketingMediaOlympicsOpinionPeople and Pop CultureSports and SocietyTechWomen's SportsSBJ TV
